mainTopic: Limits on believing someone who says 'I bought it,' who may take the robbed person's oath, the injured person's oath, and which false oaths make a person חשוד
overview: The amud opens with a ruling: someone who carries items out of a homeowner's house and says 'I bought them' is not believed. The גמרא then narrows this rule five times, and a ruling of רב הונא בר אבין and a case where רבא took items back from orphans back up the last limit. רבא rules that a watchman, and even his wife, can take the oath of a robbed person. רב פפא asks about a hired worker or harvester, and that question ends in תיקו. רב אשי rules that a robbed person can swear about a silver cup only if he is wealthy or people leave deposits with him. Next, שמואל teaches that an injured person collects without an oath if he could not have hurt himself, such as a bite on his back when no one else was there. Finally, the גמרא explains why the משנה says 'even a שבועת שוא' makes a person חשוד, and why שבועת ביטוי is not listed. A challenge about past-tense oaths gets an answer that continues on the next amud.

steps.title: A person who claims he bought the items is not believed
steps.stepSummary: Someone took items from a homeowner's house and says he bought them. He is not believed.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if he says, 'They are in my hands because I bought them,' he is not believed.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes a ruling that began just before this point. A person who took items from a homeowner and says 'I bought them' is not believed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Usually whoever holds an item gets the benefit of the doubt. Here the homeowner's ownership is clear, and the items were seen leaving his house. So the carrier's claim that he bought them is not enough. Everything that follows narrows this basic rule.

keyTerms.meaning: In my hands; in my possession

phrases.english: and he says, 'They are bought, in my hands'
he is not believed.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאָמַר לְקוּחִין הֵן בְּיָדִי אֵינוֹ נֶאֱמָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the ruling from the end of the previous section.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A person who took a homeowner's items and claims he bought them is not believed.

steps.title: First limit: only a homeowner who does not usually sell his things
steps.stepSummary: The rule applies only to a homeowner who does not usually sell his belongings. If he does sell them, the carrier is believed.
steps.simpleTranslation: We only said this about a homeowner who does not usually sell his items. But if the homeowner does usually sell his items, the carrier is believed.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins narrowing the rule. It applies only when this homeowner is not the type who sells his things.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The carrier's claim is doubted because it is unlikely this homeowner sold anything. If the homeowner often sells his belongings, a sale is very believable. So the carrier is believed.

keyTerms.meaning: We only said this when...; the formula for narrowing a rule
Homeowner; the owner of the items

phrases.english: And we only said this

phrases.aramaic: בַּעַל הַבַּיִת שֶׁאֵינוֹ עָשׂוּי לִמְכּוֹר כֵּלָיו,
phrases.english: about a homeowner who does not usually sell his items,

phrases.aramaic: אֲבָל בַּעַל הַבַּיִת הֶעָשׂוּי לִמְכּוֹר אֶת כֵּלָיו – נֶאֱמָן.
phrases.english: but with a homeowner who does usually sell his items, he is believed.
phrases.notes: 'He' is the person carrying the items, not the homeowner.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְלָא אֲמַרַן אֶלָּא בַּעַל הַבַּיִת שֶׁאֵינוֹ עָשׂוּי לִמְכּוֹר כֵּלָיו
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Narrows the ruling of step 1.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: If the homeowner usually sells his belongings, the carrier who says he bought them is believed.

steps.title: Second limit: only items that people do not usually hide
steps.stepSummary: Even with a homeowner who does not sell, the carrier is not believed only about items that are not normally hidden. With items people usually cover up, he is believed.
steps.simpleTranslation: Even with a homeowner who does not usually sell his items, we only said this about things people don't usually hide. But with things people usually hide, he is believed.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא adds a second limit. It looks at what kind of item was being carried.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Carrying an item hidden under one's clothing looks suspicious, but only if that item is normally carried in the open. If people normally cover up this kind of item, hiding it proves nothing. So the carrier is believed.

keyTerms.meaning: Their normal way; how they are usually treated

phrases.aramaic: וְשֶׁאֵין עָשׂוּי לִמְכּוֹר אֶת כֵּלָיו נָמֵי
phrases.english: And even with one who does not usually sell his items,

phrases.aramaic: – לָא אֲמַרַן אֶלָּא דְּבָרִים שֶׁאֵין דַּרְכָּן לְהַטְמִין,
phrases.english: we only said this about things that are not usually hidden,
but with things that are usually hidden, he is believed.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְשֶׁאֵין עָשׂוּי לִמְכּוֹר אֶת כֵּלָיו נָמֵי לָא אֲמַרַן אֶלָּא דְּבָרִים שֶׁאֵין דַּרְכָּן לְהַטְמִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a second limit on top of step 2.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: If the items are the kind people usually hide, the carrier is believed.

steps.title: Third limit: only a person who is not secretive
steps.stepSummary: Even with items that are not normally hidden, the carrier is not believed only if he is not a private person. A person who hides everything is just acting normally.
steps.simpleTranslation: Even with things that are not usually hidden, we only said this about a person who is not secretive. But a secretive person always does this.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא adds a third limit. Now it looks at the personality of the carrier.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Some people cover up everything they carry. For such a person, hiding an item is not a sign of guilt, because that is simply how he acts. So he too is believed.

keyTerms.meaning: Secretive; a private person who keeps things covered

phrases.english: And even with things that are not usually hidden,

phrases.aramaic: – לָא אֲמַרַן אֶלָּא אִינִישׁ דְּלָא צְנִיעַ,
phrases.english: we only said this about a person who is not secretive,
but a person who is secretive, that is just his way.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְשֶׁאֵין דַּרְכָּן לְהַטְמִין נָמֵי לָא אֲמַרַן אֶלָּא אִינִישׁ דְּלָא צְנִיעַ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a third limit on top of step 3.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A person who is secretive by nature is believed even with items that are not normally hidden.

steps.title: Fourth limit: only when the homeowner says 'borrowed,' not 'stolen'
steps.stepSummary: The rule applies when the homeowner says the items were borrowed. If he says they were stolen, he is not believed, because we do not assume a person is a thief.
steps.simpleTranslation: We only said this when one says 'borrowed' and the other says 'bought.' But if the homeowner says 'stolen,' it is not in his power to make that claim stick, because we do not assume a person is a thief.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא adds a fourth limit. It looks at what the homeowner is claiming.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Saying 'I lent it to him' is an ordinary claim, so the court takes it seriously against 'I bought it.' Saying 'he stole it' accuses the man of a crime. We do not presume people are thieves, so that accusation is not accepted.

keyTerms.meaning: It is not in his power; his word alone cannot do this
To presume; to assume someone has a certain status

steps.confusionAlert: This does not mean the homeowner loses because his case is weaker. A claim of 'stolen' is rejected because it accuses the other person of a crime, and we do not presume anyone is a thief.

phrases.english: And we only said this
when this one says 'borrowed' and that one says 'bought,'
phrases.notes: The homeowner says 'borrowed'; the carrier says 'bought.'

phrases.english: but with 'stolen,' it is not in his power;
we do not presume a person to be a thief.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְלָא אֲמַרַן אֶלָּא זֶה אוֹמֵר שְׁאוּלִין וְזֶה אוֹמֵר לְקוּחִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a fourth limit, this time about the homeowner's claim.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: If the homeowner claims the items were stolen, he is not believed, because we do not presume a person is a thief.

steps.title: Fifth limit: only items people usually lend or rent out
steps.stepSummary: The carrier is not believed only with items that are commonly lent or rented. With items people don't lend or rent, he is believed.
steps.simpleTranslation: We only said this about things that are usually lent or rented out. But with things that are not usually lent or rented out, he is believed.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא adds a fifth limit, again about the kind of item.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The homeowner's claim 'I lent it' makes sense only for items people commonly lend or rent out. For items nobody lends, it is more likely they were sold. So the carrier is believed.
steps.whatToRemember: The carrier who says 'I bought it' is not believed only when all five conditions are met. The homeowner does not usually sell, the items are not normally hidden, and the carrier is not a secretive person. The homeowner also has to claim 'borrowed' and not 'stolen,' and the items must be the kind people lend or rent out.

phrases.english: And we only said this
about things that are usually lent and rented out,

phrases.aramaic: אֲבָל דְּבָרִים שֶׁאֵין עֲשׂוּיִן לְהַשְׁאִיל וּלְהַשְׂכִּיר – נֶאֱמָן.
phrases.english: but with things that are not usually lent and rented out, he is believed.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְלָא אֲמַרַן אֶלָּא בִּדְבָרִים הָעֲשׂוּיִן לְהַשְׁאִיל וּלְהַשְׂכִּיר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a fifth limit, about whether the item is commonly lent.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: If the items are not the kind people lend or rent out, the carrier is believed.

steps.title: Support from the ruling of רב הונא בר אבין
steps.stepSummary: רב הונא בר אבין sent a ruling: with items commonly lent or rented, a person who says 'I bought them' is not believed.
steps.simpleTranslation: As רב הונא בר אבין sent: with things that are usually lent and rented out, if someone says 'They are in my hands because I bought them,' he is not believed.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a source to back up the fifth limit. רב הונא בר אבין's ruling speaks specifically about items that are lent and rented.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב הונא בר אבין worded his ruling about 'items that are usually lent and rented out.' That wording shows the rule depends on the type of item. It supports step 6.

keyTerms.meaning: Sent (a ruling, by letter or message)

phrases.english: As רב הונא בר אבין sent:
things that are usually lent and rented out,
and he says 'They are bought, in my hands,' he is not believed.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports the limit in step 6.
steps.raayaObject: That the 'not believed' rule applies to items commonly lent or rented.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The ruling sent by רב הונא בר אבין, worded about items that are usually lent and rented out.

steps.title: A real case: רבא takes scissors and a book back from orphans
steps.stepSummary: רבא took a pair of fabric scissors and a book of אגדה away from orphans, because these are items people commonly lend or rent.
steps.simpleTranslation: Like the case where רבא took a pair of tailor's scissors and a book of אגדה away from orphans, because they were things that are usually lent and rented out.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a real-life case that matches רב הונא בר אבין's ruling.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The orphans held items that were known to belong to someone else, and these were items commonly lent or rented. So רבא did not accept that their father had bought them, and he gave them back to the owner. This shows the rule being used in practice.

keyTerms.meaning: Took out; removed from someone's possession

phrases.aramaic: כִּי הָא דְּרָבָא אַפֵּיק זוּגָא דְּסַרְבָּלָא
phrases.english: Like this case where רבא took away a pair of tailor's scissors
and a book of אגדה from orphans,
phrases.notes: The orphans' father had held these items, and the real owner wanted them back.

phrases.english: because they are things that are usually lent and rented out.

steps.triggerLanguage: כִּי הָא דְּרָבָא אַפֵּיק זוּגָא דְּסַרְבָּלָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a practical example of the ruling in step 7.
steps.raayaObject: That items commonly lent or rented are returned to their known owner.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The case where רבא took scissors and a book of אגדה from orphans.

steps.title: רבא: a watchman, and even his wife, can take the oath
steps.stepSummary: רבא rules that the oath of a robbed person can be taken by the watchman of the house, and even by the watchman's wife.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: even a watchman takes the oath, and even the wife of a watchman takes the oath.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to a new topic: who may take the oath given to someone who was robbed. רבא says it does not have to be the owner himself.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The robbed person swears about what was taken from his house. רבא extends this to a watchman, who knows what was in the house. He extends it even to the watchman's wife, so the oath is not limited to the owner.

keyTerms.meaning: Watchman; one put in charge of guarding the property

steps.whyThisMatters: This widens who can take the robbed person's oath. It sets up רב פפא's question about other workers in the house.

phrases.english: רבא said:
Even a watchman takes the oath,
phrases.notes: This is the oath of a robbed person from the משנה, sworn about what was taken.

phrases.english: even the wife of a watchman takes the oath.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic about who can take the robbed person's oath.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A watchman, and even a watchman's wife, can take the oath of a robbed person.

steps.title: רב פפא asks about a hired worker or a harvester
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא asks whether the owner's regular hired worker or harvester can also take the oath.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא asked: what about his hired worker or his harvester?
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא asks how far רבא's ruling goes. He wants to know whether workers who are not guards can also swear.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A watchman was put in charge of the property, so he can swear about it. A hired worker or harvester spends time around the property but was not appointed to guard it. רב פפא asks whether that is enough.

keyTerms.meaning: Asked (a real question needing an answer)
His harvester; the one who gathers his crops

phrases.english: רב פפא asked:
His hired worker or his harvester, what is the law?

steps.triggerLanguage: בָּעֵי רַב פָּפָּא שְׂכִירוֹ וּלְקִיטוֹ מַאי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks how far רבא's ruling in step 9 reaches.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether a hired worker or harvester, who is not appointed to guard, can take the robbed person's oath.

steps.title: The question stays unresolved
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא ends with תיקו: רב פפא's question is left without an answer.
steps.simpleTranslation: Let it stand.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא cannot answer רב פפא's question, so it leaves it open.
steps.deeperAnalysis: תיקו means no proof was found either way. The status of a hired worker or harvester in this oath stays an open doubt.

keyTerms.meaning: Let it stand; the question remains unresolved

steps.whatToRemember: A watchman and his wife may take the robbed person's oath. Whether a hired worker or harvester may do so is left unresolved (תיקו).

phrases.english: Let it stand.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes רב פפא's question without an answer.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Whether a hired worker or harvester can take the robbed person's oath remains unresolved.

steps.title: What if the robbed person claims a silver cup?
steps.stepSummary: רב יימר asks רב אשי whether a robbed homeowner can swear and collect for a silver cup.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יימר said to רב אשי: If the homeowner claims that a silver cup was taken, what is the law?
steps.whatsHappening: רב יימר asks a question about the robbed person's oath from the earlier steps. Can he also swear about something expensive, like a silver cup?
steps.deeperAnalysis: Until now, the robbed person swears about what was taken and collects. A silver cup is costly, and not everyone owns one. So the question is whether we still believe his oath about such an item.

keyTerms.meaning: he made a claim against him

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב יֵימַר לְרַב אָשֵׁי:
phrases.english: Rav Yeimar said to Rav Ashi:
If he claimed against him for a silver cup, what is the law?
phrases.notes: The robbed homeowner is claiming that a silver cup was among the things taken from his house.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב יֵימַר לְרַב אָשֵׁי: טְעָנוֹ בְּכָסָא דְּכַסְפָּא, מַאי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After רב פפא's question ended in תיקו, the גמרא asks another question about the same oath of the robbed person.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does the robbed person's oath work even for an unusual, expensive item like a silver cup?

steps.title: It depends on whether he is the kind of person who would have one
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי answers: if the homeowner is wealthy, or people trust him with deposits, he swears and collects. If not, he does not.
steps.simpleTranslation: We look and see: if he is a wealthy man, or a trustworthy man with whom people leave deposits, he swears and collects. And if not, he does not.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי answers that we check what kind of person the homeowner is. If it makes sense that he had a silver cup, his oath works.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The oath only works when the claim is believable. A rich man may own a silver cup. A trusted man may be holding one for someone else. If neither is true, the claim is too unlikely, and the oath does not help him collect.

keyTerms.meaning: they deposit (leave things in his care)

steps.whatToRemember: The robbed person's oath only covers things that are believable for him to own or to hold for others.

phrases.english: We look and see:
phrases.notes: This is רב אשי's answer, even though the text does not say his name again.

phrases.english: if he is a wealthy man,
or if he is a trustworthy man
with whom people deposit things,
phrases.notes: Then the silver cup could belong to someone who left it with him.

phrases.english: he swears and takes.
And if not, not.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רב יימר's question.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: If the homeowner is wealthy, or people trust him with deposits, he swears and collects. Otherwise he does not.

steps.title: An injured person collects without an oath if he could not have hurt himself
steps.stepSummary: Quoting the משנה's case of the injured person, שמואל says the oath is needed only if he could have injured himself. If the wound is in a place he cannot reach, he collects without any oath.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה says: 'The injured person, how?' רב יהודה said in the name of שמואל: They only taught that he needs an oath where he could have injured himself. But where he could not have injured himself, he takes payment without an oath.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to a new case in the משנה, the injured person (נחבל). שמואל limits when this person has to swear.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the משנה, witnesses saw him go in healthy and come out hurt, and he swears and collects. The oath is there because maybe he hurt himself. If the wound is somewhere he could not have done it himself, that worry is gone, so no oath is needed.

keyTerms.meaning: they only taught this in the case of

phrases.english: The injured person, how?
Rav Yehuda said in the name of Shmuel:
They only taught this
in a place where he could injure himself,

phrases.aramaic: אֲבָל בִּמְקוֹם שֶׁאֵינוֹ יָכוֹל לְחַבֵּל בְּעַצְמוֹ –
phrases.english: but in a place where he cannot injure himself,
he takes payment without an oath.

steps.triggerLanguage: נֶחְבָּל כֵּיצַד. אָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה אָמַר שְׁמוּאֵל: לֹא שָׁנוּ אֶלָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new case from the משנה: the injured person.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The oath is needed only where he could have hurt himself. Where he could not, he collects without an oath.

steps.title: Maybe he rubbed against a wall
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks: even in a hard-to-reach place, maybe he hurt himself by scraping against a wall.
steps.simpleTranslation: But let us worry that perhaps he rubbed himself against a wall!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges שמואל. A person can hurt any part of his body by rubbing it against a wall.
steps.deeperAnalysis: שמואל's rule depends on there being places a person cannot injure himself. The challenge says there are no such places, because a wall can scrape anywhere. If so, the oath should always be needed.

phrases.english: But let us worry that perhaps he rubbed against a wall!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges שמואל's idea of a place where he cannot hurt himself.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A wall can scrape any part of the body, so there is no truly unreachable place.

steps.title: A bite on his back or elbows
steps.stepSummary: רבי חייא teaches that the case is a bite on his back or between his elbows. A wall cannot make a bite.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי חייא taught: the case is where a bite appeared on his back or between his elbows.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers with a ברייתא of רבי חייא. The wound is a bite in a place he cannot reach with his own mouth.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A wall can scrape, but it cannot leave a bite mark. A person also cannot bite his own back or elbows. So he clearly did not do this to himself.

phrases.english: Rabbi Chiya taught:
that a bite appeared on him
on his back or between his elbows.
phrases.notes: He cannot bite himself in these spots, and a wall does not leave bite marks.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the wall challenge.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Any wound could have come from scraping against a wall.
steps.terutzMaskana: The case is a bite in a spot he cannot reach, which he could not have caused himself.

steps.title: Maybe someone else bit him
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks: even if he did not do it himself, maybe a different person did it, not the defendant.
steps.simpleTranslation: But perhaps someone else did it to him?
steps.whatsHappening: A new challenge. Fine, he did not hurt himself, but why blame this defendant?
steps.deeperAnalysis: Ruling out self-injury is not enough to make this defendant pay. Some other person could have caused the bite.

phrases.english: But perhaps someone else did it to him?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Accepts the bite answer, then raises a new doubt.
steps.kashyaTarget: Collecting from the defendant without an oath
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Someone other than the defendant may have caused the injury.

steps.title: No one else was there
steps.stepSummary: The case is where no other person was present besides the defendant.
steps.simpleTranslation: The case is where there is no one else.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that only the defendant was with him, so nobody else could have done it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Two possibilities are now ruled out: he did not hurt himself, and nobody else was there. That leaves only the defendant, so the injured person collects without an oath.
steps.whatToRemember: An injured person collects without an oath only when he could not have hurt himself (for example, a bite on his back) and no one else besides the defendant was there.

phrases.english: Where there is no one else.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the 'someone else' challenge.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Another person may have caused the bite.
steps.terutzMaskana: The case is where only the defendant was present.

steps.title: Why does the משנה say 'even a שבועת שוא'?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה's case of an opponent who is חשוד on oaths, including 'even a שבועת שוא', and asks what that phrase comes to add.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה says: 'And when his opponent is suspect,' and so on, 'and even a vain oath.' What does 'even a vain oath' mean?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to the next case in the משנה, an opponent who cannot be trusted with an oath. It asks why the משנה adds 'even a שבועת שוא'. This sets up the next step, where the answer will come.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the משנה, someone who swore falsely loses the right to swear. Then the other side swears and collects instead. The משנה says this applies even to a שבועת שוא, a pointless oath. The גמרא wants to know why such a lighter oath would make a person suspect.

phrases.english: And when his opponent is suspect, etc.
phrases.notes: The words of the משנה. 'Etc.' means the rest of the משנה's line, which is skipped here.

phrases.english: and even a vain oath.
What is meant by "even a vain oath"?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new case from the משנה: the opponent who is חשוד on oaths.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why does even a שבועת שוא make a person חשוד, so that he is not allowed to swear?

steps.title: The משנה builds from obvious to less obvious
steps.stepSummary: The phrase 'even a שבועת שוא' teaches a 'לא מיבעיא': not only false oaths about money, but even an oath that only denies words makes a person untrustworthy.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה is speaking in the style of 'it is not necessary.' It is not necessary to say this about those oaths, which involve denying money. But even this one, which is only a denial of words, also makes him not believed.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question from step 19. The word 'even' shows the משנה is moving from an obvious case to a less obvious one.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The other oaths in the list, like שבועת הפקדון and שבועת העדות, involve denying someone's money. A שבועת שוא costs nobody anything, so you might think it does not ruin his trust. The משנה teaches that even this makes him חשוד.

keyTerms.meaning: It is not necessary to say; a style that goes from the obvious case to the bigger חידוש
Denying money owed to someone else
Denying mere words, with no money involved
He is not believed or trusted

steps.confusionAlert: 'Even' does not mean שבועת שוא is worse than the others. It means it is the least obvious case, so you might have thought it does not count.

phrases.english: It is speaking in the style of 'it is not necessary':
It is not necessary to say this about those oaths,
phrases.notes: 'Those' means the other oaths the משנה listed before 'even a שבועת שוא.'

phrases.english: which involve denying money;
but even this one too,
which is only a denial of words,
he is not believed.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 19 about what 'even a שבועת שוא' adds.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What the word 'even' before שבועת שוא comes to add.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: It teaches that even an oath without any money denial makes a person חשוד על השבועה.

steps.title: Why not also list the oath of utterance?
steps.stepSummary: If an oath with no money involved counts, the משנה should also list שבועת ביטוי.
steps.simpleTranslation: Then let the משנה also teach שבועת ביטוי!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the משנה: if non-money oaths count, why is שבועת ביטוי left out?
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 20 said that even a word-only oath like שבועת שוא makes someone חשוד. A שבועת ביטוי, like 'I will eat' or 'I will not eat,' is also a word-only oath. So it seems it should be on the list too.

keyTerms.meaning: An oath of utterance, such as swearing 'I will eat' or 'I ate'

phrases.english: Then let it also teach an oath of utterance!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on the answer of step 20 and finds a missing case.
steps.kashyaTarget: The list of oaths in the משנה
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If a word-only oath is enough to make one חשוד, שבועת ביטוי is also a word-only oath and should be listed.

steps.title: Only oaths that are false when spoken are listed
steps.stepSummary: The משנה lists only oaths that are a lie at the moment they are said. A שבועת ביטוי about the future may have been meant truthfully.
steps.simpleTranslation: When the משנה teaches, it teaches an oath where, when he swears, he is swearing falsely. But a שבועת ביטוי, where one can say he swore truthfully, it does not teach.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the משנה only lists oaths that are a lie at the very moment they are said.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If someone swears 'I will eat this,' he may have fully meant it and only later failed to do it. That is not a knowing lie, so it does not show he is a liar. The other oaths on the list are false right when he says them.

phrases.english: When it teaches, it teaches an oath

phrases.aramaic: דְּכִי קָא מִשְׁתְּבַע – בְּשִׁקְרָא קָא מִשְׁתְּבַע;
phrases.english: where, when he swears, he swears falsely;
but an oath of utterance,
where it can be said
that he swore truthfully,
it does not teach.

steps.triggerLanguage: כִּי קָתָנֵי, שְׁבוּעָה דְּכִי קָא מִשְׁתְּבַע בְּשִׁקְרָא קָא מִשְׁתְּבַע
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 21.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Defines the rule behind the list: only oaths false when spoken
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Every word-only false oath, including שבועת ביטוי, should make one חשוד.
steps.terutzMaskana: Only an oath that is a lie at the moment of swearing makes one חשוד. A future promise may have been sincere.

steps.title: What about an oath about the past?
steps.stepSummary: The answer works for future oaths, but an oath like 'I ate' is false right away, so why is it not listed?
steps.simpleTranslation: This works well for 'I will eat' and 'I will not eat.' But for 'I ate' and 'I did not eat,' what is there to say?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the answer of step 22: it only covers oaths about the future.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A שבועת ביטוי can also be about the past. If he swears 'I ate' and he did not, he knew it was a lie when he said it. So by the rule of step 22, this kind should be listed in the משנה.

keyTerms.meaning: It works well for; this is fine for
I will eat / I will not eat; an oath about the future
I ate / I did not eat; an oath about the past

phrases.english: This works well for 'I will eat' and 'I will not eat';
but for 'I ate' and 'I did not eat'
what is there to say?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the answer of step 22 as covering only future oaths.
steps.kashyaTarget: The answer that שבועת ביטוי may have been sworn truthfully
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A past-tense שבועת ביטוי is false when spoken, so by the גמרא's own rule it should be listed.

steps.title: Reading 'oath in vain' differently
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא begins its answer by telling us to read the משנה's phrase שבועת שוא in a certain way. The answer continues on the next amud.
steps.simpleTranslation: Teach the משנה's words 'an oath in vain'...
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts answering the challenge of step 23 by rereading the phrase שבועת שוא in the משנה. This line opens the answer, and the explanation continues on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Instead of adding a new case to the משנה, the גמרא suggests the past-tense שבועת ביטוי may already be hinted at inside the words שבועת שוא. The full explanation comes on the next amud.

keyTerms.meaning: Teach it as; read the משנה this way
An oath in vain, a pointless or obviously false oath

phrases.english: Teach 'an oath in vain'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins the answer to the challenge of step 23.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Rereading the wording of the משנה
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The משנה left out the past-tense שבועת ביטוי entirely.
steps.terutzMaskana: The answer starts by reading the phrase שבועת שוא in a new way; it is completed in the continuation.
